steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper comparing task formulations for timeline construction with LLMs. Motivate the task, explain what is missing in time anchoring and pairwise temporal ordering work, introduce our new dataset and evaluation framework, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Timeline construction: task and applications
2. Time anchoring approach and its limits
3. Event temporal ordering as a context-based task; existing formulations
4. Open question: which task formulation best elicits LLM capabilities?
5. Our dataset (TimeSET) and evaluation framework
6. Benchmarking open LLMs on existing datasets
7. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Timeline construction
- structure events in chronological order from textual input
- applications: assisting well-informed decisions, text analysis, script induction
- news articles: events not always described in chronological order
- Figure 1 example: “ban” mentioned before “doping”, but order is doping -> ban

2. Time anchoring
- prior work: identify each event's time expression as its anchor, compare anchors to order events
- problem: sequential events can be anchored to the same coarse time range
- Figure 1: “testing” and “loss” both anchored to “February”; true order loss -> testing
- handling this needs comprehension of context

3. Event temporal ordering
- context-based, no exclusive attention to time expressions
- conventionally pairwise classification: covers every pair, but annotation cost for \binom{n}{2} pairs grows with number of events n (unlike time anchoring)
- in practice only local pairs annotated (e.g., adjacent sentences) -> datasets suboptimal for evaluating timeline construction
- other formulations: NLI (TemporalNLI), MRC (TORQUE)

4. Open question
- models only comparable within one dataset / its formulation; no cross-dataset comparison
- several datasets assess same capability -> which task formulation best elicits capabilities of models?
- more important with LLMs, evaluated on multiple datasets few-shot
- Figure 1: one pairwise relation at a time (“Relation between ban and retired is”, “AFTER”) vs multiple relations in one QA pair (“What happened after testing?” “retired, ban”)

5. TimeSET and evaluation framework
- TimeSET (Time line for S alient E ven T s): lack of testbed for context-based timeline construction
- Wikinews articles, diverse topics; single-document timeline annotation from document-level pairwise orders
- practical workload: saliency-based event selection (IE ~ Summarization), partial-order annotation (script annotation) -> Section 3
- framework: four formulations NLI, Pairwise, MRC, Timeline; same document-timeline pair, each prompts LLMs its own way, different number of times
- intuition: LLMs favor formulation close to tasks seen in pretraining / tuning
- RQ1: which formulation better elicits LLMs' capabilities? open LLMs: Llama 2, Flan-T5 -> Section 4

6. Benchmarking
- RQ2: how good are open LLMs at identifying order of events?
- datasets: TemporalNLI, MATRES, TDDiscourse, TORQUE
- event temporal ordering = core subtask of timeline construction
- in-context learning vs smaller fine-tuned models -> Section 5

7. Contributions (three)
- TimeSET dataset, open license
- framework for cross-model / cross-formulation comparison; NLI + Flan-T5 strong
- few-shot open LLMs underperform smaller fine-tuned models on existing datasets

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Timeline construction is the task of putting events in chronological order based on a text. It is useful for practical applications such as helping people make well-informed decisions, text analysis, or script induction. In news articles, events are not always described in the order they happened. For example, in Figure 1:

“ ban ” is mentioned before “ doping ”, but the temporal order is “ doping ” \rightarrow “ ban.”

Previous work has treated timeline construction as a time anchoring task, where each event is anchored to its corresponding time expression and then the anchors are compared to order the events. The problem is that sequential events can be anchored to the same coarse time range. Also in Figure 1:

both “ testing ” and “ loss ” are anchored to “ February,” which does not capture the temporal order, “ loss ” \rightarrow “ testing.” To handle cases like this you need to understand the context.

At the same time, event temporal ordering has been studied a lot as a context-based task that does not focus only on time expressions. Usually event temporal ordering is set up as a pairwise classification task. This can cover every pair, but annotating \binom{n}{2} pairs becomes expensive when the number of events n increases, which is not the case for the time anchoring approach. So in practice previous work only looks at local pairs (e.g., within adjacent sentences) to keep the cost down, and this makes the datasets not ideal for evaluating timeline construction systems.

Other task formulations have also been explored to test models on event temporal reasoning, for example Natural Language Inference (NLI) in TemporalNLI or Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) in TORQUE.

Basically, models can only be compared inside one dataset with its own task formulation, and comparing models across datasets is not supported. Since several datasets test the same event temporal ordering capability, a question comes up: Which task formulation best elicits the capabilities of models? This question is even more important now with LLMs, which can be evaluated on multiple datasets in a few-shot setting. As shown in Figure 1, LLMs can be prompted to find one pairwise relation at a time (e.g., “ Relation between ban and retired is ”, “ AFTER ”) or several relations in one question-answer pair (e.g., “ What happened after testing? ” “ retired, ban ”).

5. TimeSET and evaluation framework
- TimeSET (Time line for S alient E ven T s): lack of testbed for context-based timeline construction
- Wikinews articles, diverse topics; single-document timeline annotation from document-level pairwise orders
- practical workload: saliency-based event selection (IE ~ Summarization), partial-order annotation (script annotation) -> Section 3
- framework: four formulations NLI, Pairwise, MRC, Timeline; same document-timeline pair, each prompts LLMs its own way, different number of times
- intuition: LLMs favor formulation close to tasks seen in pretraining / tuning
- RQ1: which formulation better elicits LLMs' capabilities? open LLMs: Llama 2, Flan-T5 -> Section 4

6. Benchmarking
- RQ2: how good are open LLMs at identifying order of events?
- datasets: TemporalNLI, MATRES, TDDiscourse, TORQUE
- event temporal ordering = core subtask of timeline construction
- in-context learning vs smaller fine-tuned models -> Section 5

7. Contributions (three)
- TimeSET dataset, open license
- framework for cross-model / cross-formulation comparison; NLI + Flan-T5 strong
- few-shot open LLMs underperform smaller fine-tuned models on existing datasets

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Timeline construction is the task of putting events in chronological order based on a text. It is useful for practical applications such as helping people make well-informed decisions, text analysis, or script induction. In news articles, events are not always described in the order they happened. For example, in Figure 1:

“ ban ” is mentioned before “ doping ”, but the temporal order is “ doping ” \rightarrow “ ban.”

Previous work has treated timeline construction as a time anchoring task, where each event is anchored to its corresponding time expression and then the anchors are compared to order the events. The problem is that sequential events can be anchored to the same coarse time range. Also in Figure 1:

both “ testing ” and “ loss ” are anchored to “ February,” which does not capture the temporal order, “ loss ” \rightarrow “ testing.” To handle cases like this you need to understand the context.

At the same time, event temporal ordering has been studied a lot as a context-based task that does not focus only on time expressions. Usually event temporal ordering is set up as a pairwise classification task. This can cover every pair, but annotating \binom{n}{2} pairs becomes expensive when the number of events n increases, which is not the case for the time anchoring approach. So in practice previous work only looks at local pairs (e.g., within adjacent sentences) to keep the cost down, and this makes the datasets not ideal for evaluating timeline construction systems.

Other task formulations have also been explored to test models on event temporal reasoning, for example Natural Language Inference (NLI) in TemporalNLI or Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) in TORQUE.

Basically, models can only be compared inside one dataset with its own task formulation, and comparing models across datasets is not supported. Since several datasets test the same event temporal ordering capability, a question comes up: Which task formulation best elicits the capabilities of models? This question is even more important now with LLMs, which can be evaluated on multiple datasets in a few-shot setting. As shown in Figure 1, LLMs can be prompted to find one pairwise relation at a time (e.g., “ Relation between ban and retired is ”, “ AFTER ”) or several relations in one question-answer pair (e.g., “ What happened after testing? ” “ retired, ban ”).

In this paper, we first propose a new evaluation dataset, TimeSET (Time line for S alient E ven T s), because there is no testbed for context-based timeline construction. TimeSET has Wikinews articles on diverse topics, with single-document timeline annotation based on document-level pairwise orders. To make the annotation workload practical, TimeSET has two features: saliency-based event selection, which is motivated by the similarity between Information Extraction (IE) and Summarization, and partial-order annotation, which is inspired by script annotation (Section 3).

Second, we propose a new evaluation framework for timeline construction that lets us compare across models and task formulations. We cast TimeSET into four task formulations: Natural Language Inference (NLI), Pairwise, Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC), and Timeline (see Figure 1). For the same document-timeline pair, each formulation prompts LLMs in its own way and a different number of times to find the temporal orders of a timeline from a document. Our intuition is that LLMs will favor one formulation over the others depending on how close it is to the tasks they saw during pretraining or tuning. Using this framework we answer our first research question, (1) “Which task formulation better elicits LLMs’ capabilities for timeline construction?,” focusing on open LLMs (i.e., Llama 2 and Flan-T5) (Section 4).

We also answer a second research question, (2) “How good are open LLMs at identifying the order of events?,” by benchmarking open LLMs on existing datasets: TemporalNLI, MATRES, TDDiscourse, and TORQUE. Event temporal ordering is a core subtask of timeline construction, so benchmarking open LLMs in in-context learning and comparing them with smaller fine-tuned models helps to get robust insights for developing timeline construction systems further (Section 5).

To summarize, we have three contributions:

- • We develop a new evaluation dataset, TimeSET, for context-based timeline construction. The dataset is available under an open license.

- • For research question (1), we propose a new evaluation framework that allows comparisons across models and across formulations. Our experiment with TimeSET shows that the NLI formulation with Flan-T5 performs strongly compared to the others.

- • For research question (2), we benchmark open LLMs in a few-shot setting on existing event temporal ordering datasets. We find that few-shot LLMs do worse than smaller fine-tuned models.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Timeline construction requires structuring events in chronological order based on textual input. The task has implications for practical applications, such as assisting well-informed decisions [1], text analysis [2], or script induction [3]. In a news article, events are not always described in chronological order [4]. For instance, from Figure 1:

“ ban ” is mentioned before “ doping ”, but the temporal order is “ doping ” \rightarrow “ ban.”

Prior work has addressed timeline construction as a time anchoring task: identify the time expression corresponding to each event as its anchor, and compare the anchors to order the events [5]. However, sequential events can be anchored to the same coarse time range [6]. Also from Figure 1:

both “ testing ” and “ loss ” are anchored to “ February,” which fails to capture the temporal order, “ loss ” \rightarrow “ testing.” Handling such cases requires comprehension of the context.

In parallel, event temporal ordering has been actively explored as a context-based task that does not focus exclusively on time expressions. Conventionally, event temporal ordering is formulated as a pairwise classification task. While this approach can cover every pair, the annotation cost for \binom{n}{2} pairs gets expensive as the number of events n increases, unlike the time anchoring approach [7]. In practice, previous work focuses only on local pairs (e.g., within adjacent sentences) to reduce the cost [8], which makes these datasets suboptimal for evaluating timeline construction systems.

In terms of task design, other formulations, such as Natural Language Inference (NLI) by TemporalNLI [9] or Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) by TORQUE [10], have also been explored to assess models’ capabilities on event temporal reasoning.

In principle, models can only be compared within one dataset based on its task formulation; comparing models across datasets is not supported. Given that multiple datasets assess the same event temporal ordering capability, one question arises: Which task formulation best elicits the capabilities of models? This question becomes more important with the surge of LLMs, which can be evaluated on multiple datasets in a few-shot setting. More specifically, as shown in Figure 1, LLMs can be prompted to identify one pairwise relation at a time (e.g., “ Relation between ban and retired is ”, “ AFTER ”) or multiple relations in one question-answer pair (e.g., “ What happened after testing? ” “ retired, ban ”).

In this paper, we first propose a new evaluation dataset, TimeSET (Time line for S alient E ven T s), to address the lack of a testbed for context-based timeline construction. TimeSET consists of Wikinews articles on diverse topics with single-document timeline annotation based on document-level pairwise orders. We introduce two features in TimeSET that enable a practical annotation workload: saliency-based event selection, motivated by the similarity between Information Extraction (IE) and Summarization [11], and partial-order annotation, inspired by script annotation [12] (Section 3).

Second, we propose a novel evaluation framework for timeline construction that enables comparison across models and task formulations. Specifically, we cast TimeSET into four task formulations, Natural Language Inference (NLI), Pairwise, Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC), and Timeline (illustrated in Figure 1). For the same document-timeline pair, each formulation prompts LLMs in its own manner, a different number of times, to identify the temporal orders of a timeline from a document. Intuitively, LLMs should favor one formulation over the others depending on how close it is to the tasks they were exposed to during pretraining or tuning. With this framework, we address our first research question, (1) “Which task formulation better elicits LLMs’ capabilities for timeline construction?,” targeting open LLMs in particular (i.e., Llama 2 [13] and Flan-T5 [14]) (Section 4).

We further address our second research question, (2) “How good are open LLMs at identifying the order of events?,” by benchmarking open LLMs on existing datasets, namely TemporalNLI, MATRES [8], TDDiscourse [6], and TORQUE. Since event temporal ordering is a core subtask of timeline construction, benchmarking open LLMs in in-context learning [15] and comparing them with smaller fine-tuned models helps us gain robust insights for the further development of timeline construction systems (Section 5).

In summary, our contributions are three-fold:

- • We develop a new evaluation dataset, TimeSET, to support context-based timeline construction. The dataset is available under an open license.

- • For research question (1), we propose a novel evaluation framework that enables cross-model and cross-formulation comparisons. Our experiment on TimeSET indicates that the NLI formulation with Flan-T5 shows strong performance among the others.

- • For research question (2), we benchmark open LLMs in a few-shot setting on existing event temporal ordering datasets. We find that few-shot LLMs underperform smaller fine-tuned models.
